You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: H4422

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "Slip away, escape; in Piel, deliver or rescue; in rare usage, bring forth or lay eggs."
  Readable gloss: "Built on the root idea of slipping free, this verb captures both self-initiated escape and divinely granted deliverance. In the Nifal, it describes fleeing from danger — Lot escaping Sodom (Gen 19:17, 22), Ehud slipping away after his assassination of Eglon (Judg 3:26), or David eluding Saul's pursuit (1 Sam 19:10). The Piel shifts to causative rescue: God or a human agent delivers another from death or captivity, as when Michal saves David's life (1 Sam 19:11). A surprising specialized sense appears in Isaiah 34:15 and 66:7, where the verb means to bring forth young or lay eggs — perhaps from the image of something 'slipping out.' Arabic cognates confirm the core meaning of slipping free."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "Nifal: escape, flee"
    Enriched: Nifal: to escape, slip away, flee from danger or pursuit. The most frequent sense, covering self-extrication from mortal peril. Lot flees the destruction of Sodom (Gen 19:17, 20, 22); Ehud escapes to Seirah (Judg 3:26); the psalmist's soul escapes like a bird from a snare (Ps 124:7). Arabic مَلَصَ 'slip from the hand' illuminates the core image. Korean 도망치다/피하다 and Swahili -toroka capture the urge...
    Existing Spanish translations: escapará, escapó, y-escapé, y-escapó
  Sense 2: "Piel: deliver, rescue"
    Enriched: Piel causative: to deliver, rescue, save someone from danger, death, or captivity. The agent actively effects another's deliverance. Michal delivers David from Saul (1 Sam 19:11); God promises to rescue the faithful (Ps 18:48, 2 Sam 22:49). Spanish 'librar' and German 'erretten/retten' both highlight the rescue dimension absent from the intransitive Nifal escape sense.
    Existing Spanish translations: ciertamente-librar, escapará, escapará., libra, libraba, librar, librará, libró., lo-librará, los-que-libraron, salvando, te-libraré, y-libró, y-salva, y-salven
  Sense 3: "Hitpael: escape oneself"
    Enriched: Hitpael reflexive: to deliver or extricate oneself by one's own effort. Rare (Job 19:20, 41:19), this intensified reflexive emphasizes personal agency in escaping. Job laments that he escaped 'by the skin of my teeth' (Job 19:20) — the barest margin of self-rescue. Swahili -okolewa captures this reflexive survival nuance.
    Existing Spanish translations: escapan, y-he-escapado
  Sense 4: "Piel/Hifil: bring forth, lay eggs"
    Enriched: Piel/Hifil specialized: to bring forth young, to lay eggs. An unexpected biological extension of the 'slip out' image, found only in Isaiah 34:15 (an arrow-snake laying and hatching eggs) and Isaiah 66:7 (Zion delivering before labor). Spanish 'dar a luz' (give birth) and Swahili -zaa show how translators shift entirely from escape to parturition vocabulary for these passages.
    Existing Spanish translations: y-dio-a-luz, y-pondrá-huevos
  Sense 5: ""
    Enriched: A single Hifil participle occurrence in Isaiah 31:5 describing YHWH 'delivering' Jerusalem — functioning as a causative rescue parallel to sense 2 but in participial form. English 'rescuing' and Spanish 'haciendo escapar' treat it as an active deliverance in progress, consistent with the broader Piel/Hifil rescue usage.
    Existing Spanish translations: y-haciendo-escapar
